entries.label: a folded function map nested under an at-rule in a createTheme override
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 31, the level the reorder had to reach
entries.note: The missing-`default` check reaches every level of a value, not only the top one, as the reference implementation's recursion does. Checking only the top level left a fold one level down reading the sentence about zero-argument functions, which is the defect the reorder is for.

entries.label: every falsy value as a ternary test, beside the same value under `||`
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 39, the two truthiness tables
entries.note: A ternary read its test through a second truthiness table beside the coercion crate's, and the copy had drifted: its numeric arm asked `n.value != 0.0`, the one comparison `NaN` answers true. So `NaN ? a : b` chose the consequent while `NaN || x` chose `x`, on the same value -- which is why the logical row sits in the same entry. The negative and tilde rows are the second table's unary arms, which read an arithmetic operator as a negation.

entries.label: an array, an object, a function and a fold as a ternary test
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 39, found while deleting the second table
entries.note: The truthiness question asked of a value the evaluator holds in a shape with no expression form: an array is its own vector and a fold is a function map. Each stands for an object, every object is truthy, and both askers used to require an expression form and refuse the build instead -- on tests the language has no doubt about.

entries.label: `Object.keys`, `values` and `entries` of the folded namespace map
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 40, the third reader of the fold
entries.note: The receiver normalizer had no arm for a folded function map, so it read as "not an object" and `Object.keys(stylex)` answered `[]` -- neither a refusal nor the truth, while the spread arm answered the keys correctly one function away. All three readers go through `function_fold_to_object` now, and the fold carries `env` beside `when`, so the keys, the values and the entries all agree with upstream. `env` reaching the fold took widening the map's value type: it is an object of the `env` option's entries, not a function config, and only the member-expression map beside the fold could hold one.

entries.label: `Object.keys` of `null`, in a template and behind a length read
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 40, found while measuring the three methods
entries.note: `null` and `undefined` have no `ToObject`, so the language throws where every other non-object receiver answers `[]`. This folded to the empty list before -- CSS the source does not describe, written quietly in both rows -- and refuses now, with the `TypeError` the language raises rather than a sentence about arrays. The two sentences stopped matching when the `Object` statics moved to the engine: the refusal is the engine's own throw now, worded `cannot convert 'null' or 'undefined' to object` where the reference compiler's runtime says `Cannot convert undefined or null to object`. Both name the receiver, which is what an author acts on, and neither compiler builds the module.

entries.label: `Object.keys` of an array carrying a hole
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 40, found while measuring every receiver
entries.note: Divergent in this compiler's favour. `Object.keys([, 'p'])` is `['1']` -- a hole has no key of its own -- and that is what this answers. Upstream aborts the module with `Unexpected error:`, reading the hole as a node and failing on it.

entries.label: `Object.values` and `Object.entries` of a single folded config
entries.origin: issue #1266, ticket 40, the half of the single-config receiver that does not fold
entries.note: `Object.keys` of a single config folds and agrees -- both compilers answer `fn` -- and the value at that key is the function the config wraps. A function's `ToString` is its source text, and this evaluator keeps none, so it refuses. Divergent deliberately: upstream answers the source text of its own implementation, which hashes a class name off text no author wrote and no two versions of the compiler spell alike. A refusal is loud where that is silent. Kept as a row so the choice is measured rather than assumed, and so the day either side moves it reports.

entries.label: a `@media` breakpoint chain at fractional `rem`, whose upper bounds are derived
entries.origin: issue #1267, the reported reproduction verbatim
entries.note: The one subject in the corpus that asks the media-query transform to derive a bound rather than to carry a condition key. Last-media-query-wins closes each range at `next - 0.01`, and `28.81 - 0.01` is `28.799999999999997` in double precision and `28.8` in single -- so a narrowing regression moves the query text, the class hash, and this verdict. Recorded `identical` because that is what a run reads: the pinning is what makes a later disagreement loud.

entries.label: a strict range `@media` query, whose two bounds are nudged
entries.origin: issue #1267, the range-syntax path into the same arithmetic
entries.note: Range syntax reaches the nudge by a different path from the breakpoint chain: a strict bound is rewritten to a `min-`/`max-` pair by moving each end 0.01, rather than by looking at the next rule. Both ends are asked here, since a one-sided rewrite would still agree on the other.

entries.label: a `@container` query at a fractional bound
entries.origin: issue #1267, the container-query path into the same arithmetic
entries.note: What a run reads here is that neither compiler transforms a container query at all: both echo `@container (min-width: 28.81px)` and `@container (width > 400.5px)` as authored, where the same two shapes under `@media` become a derived range and a nudged `min-`/`max-` pair. Kept because that is the agreement worth pinning -- the at-rule name is what selects the path, so a change that widened the media rewrite to reach `@container` would move this row and nothing in the media rows.

entries.label: a `@supports` condition nested with a `@media` chain
entries.origin: issue #1267, a derived bound reached below a non-media condition
entries.note: A `@supports` condition carries no length to normalize, which is the point: it is the wrapper the media chain is derived *inside*, so this asks whether the transform still runs one level down. It does, and inexactly -- the derived bound reads `2.1900000000000004rem`, so the row measures the digits as well as the reach.

entries.label: a ladder of exclusive `@media` breakpoints ending in a `max-width`-only rung
entries.origin: issue #1268, the reported reproduction verbatim
entries.note: No two rungs touch, so every branch the negation chain distributes into contradicts. A contradiction is retained rather than pruned -- it prints as `not all`, and the disjunction nesting around it stays in the key that the class name hashes. Two of the seven class names here depend on that wrapper, which is why the subject belongs in the corpus rather than only in the Rust suites: it is the seam that fails when the reference implementation moves rather than when this compiler does.

entries.label: two `@media` entries of one value map that canonicalize to the same query
entries.origin: issue #1268, the second divergence the first one exposes
entries.note: Rewritten keys are written into a map, so the second entry to reach a key replaces the first entry's value and keeps its position -- and one authored declaration, `red`, is absent from the output. The collision straddles the `min-height` key, so the surviving position is observable rather than incidental. Recorded here rather than only in the Rust suites because the rule count is the thing being compared, and this is the seam that compares it against the reference implementation instead of against our own belief about it.

entries.label: a `@media` list whose comma segments each hold their own combinator
entries.origin: issue #1268, ticket 13 -- the grammar sweep
entries.note: Comma and `or` both mean disjunction and both reach the same `Or` node, but `or` groups inside a comma segment and the segments group above it. The last-media-query-wins transform distributes negations over whatever the top-level `Or` holds, so flattening the two spread them over the wrong number of disjuncts and emitted a different rule under a different class name -- with both compilers accepting the query and neither saying anything.

entries.label: a `@media` disjunction inside parentheses, in each position it can take
entries.origin: issue #1268, ticket 13 -- the grammar sweep
entries.note: `( <media-condition> )` is a media query in its own right and a condition may hold an `or`, so all three are valid CSS -- and this compiler refused them. Worth pinning for the second half too: the parentheses that made the query parseable do not survive serialization, so the middle key prints as though the `and` bound tighter than the `or`. That is the reference implementation's output and the class name hashes it.

entries.label: an accented attribute selector nested between two ASCII neighbours
entries.origin: the reported shape of the collation divergence, three keys rather than two
entries.note: The shape the divergence was reported as, and the one a pseudo-name row cannot ask: an accented key has to land *between* two others for the ordering to be visible rather than merely reversed. Every pseudo name CSS defines is ASCII, so an attribute selector is also the only way a non-ASCII key reaches the comparator at all -- through the attribute name here, and through a quoted attribute value in general, which is what makes the reachable set unbounded.

entries.label: an unresolvable binding spread into the style object
entries.origin: issue #1266, the spread shape that is not the reported one
entries.note: Here because the reported spread is a shadowed dynamic parameter, and the complaint a spread earns was changed for the position rather than for that binding. This asks whether the change was right for a spread whose value fails to resolve for an entirely different reason, and the answer read from a run is that it was: upstream writes the same sentence for this shape too. Without this row the rule would rest on one subject.

entries.label: a hoisted function declaration spread into the style object
entries.origin: issue #1266, a spread whose binding resolves to something with no keys to enumerate
entries.note: The third spread shape, and the one where the binding resolves fine: a function declaration is a value, it just has no keys a style object can take. Read from a run, both compilers name the call rather than the binding -- so the complaint a spread earns is about the position on both sides, whatever the spread resolved to. The computed-key subject beside these still names the binding, which is what keeps this a rule about spreads rather than about refusals generally.

entries.label: a static spread folded into a dynamic style body
entries.origin: the spread arm of evaluate_partial_object_recursively
entries.note: A spread whose operand folds contributes that value's keys and the fold carries on, which is `Object.assign(obj, result.value)` upstream. This compiler used to refuse it outright, so a program the reference compiler compiles did not build. Pinned as an agreement rather than left to a snapshot, because the snapshot cannot notice the reference compiler moving.

entries.label: a spread and an authored key colliding, spread first
entries.origin: the spread arm of evaluate_partial_object_recursively
entries.note: `Object.assign` is last-wins, so the authored `color` after the spread takes it: blue, not red. The direction is the half of the merge a fixture has to carry, and the sibling entry below runs it the other way round.

entries.label: a spread and an authored key colliding, spread last
entries.origin: the spread arm of evaluate_partial_object_recursively
entries.note: The same collision the other way: the spread is later, so `red` wins. The key also keeps the position the authored `color` gave it rather than moving to where the spread sits, which is what `assign_props` means by keeping the first position.

entries.label: a static spread folded one level down, under a pseudo
entries.origin: the spread arm of evaluate_partial_object_recursively, reached through the recursion
entries.note: Nesting is what a style object is mostly made of, so a spread that folded only at the top would be the more misleading half-fix. This is the recursive call reaching the same arm.

entries.label: the string methods a static receiver answers
entries.origin: issue 06, the string half of the divergence table

entries.label: the array methods a static receiver answers
entries.origin: issue 06, the array half of the divergence table

entries.label: a chain folded at every link
entries.origin: issue 06, the shape two separate method tables cannot agree on

entries.label: the object prototype reached by reflection
entries.origin: issue 06, the object row of the divergence table

entries.label: NaN and Infinity reaching a declaration
entries.origin: issue 06, the parity-versus-useful-refusal choice

entries.label: a mutating array method on a value written out
entries.origin: issue 06, the mutation divergence held deliberately, reversed
entries.note: Agreement now, and the row that says the divergence was closed rather than forgotten. It read `acceptance-divergent` while a mutating method was refused here on the reasoning that matching upstream would carry mutation into a pure evaluator. Measured, upstream does not refuse mutating methods at all: it folds them on any receiver not reachable by name and disqualifies the *binding* instead, so the engine only ever mutates a temporary nothing can name afterwards. `modules-mutated-binding-read-through-a-method-call` is the other half -- the rule that does the work, and where both compilers still refuse.

entries.label: a mutated binding read as a method receiver, above and below the mutation
entries.origin: the rule that replaces the mutating-method refusal
entries.note: The mutation disqualifies the binding, not the method, and it does so for the whole file: this read sits *above* the `sort()` and still refuses on both compilers. Upstream's mutation test walks a binding's references with no position check, so agreeing here is what keeps the two builds from naming different classes for one authored style. `modules-06-mutating-array-method` is the same method with no binding involved, where both fold. Both refuse, in different words: upstream reports `Unsupported expression: CallExpression`, having dropped the receiver's own reason with the state it evaluated it under, where this compiler carries the rule up and names the binding. Message text is not a parity obligation, and the sentence that names the rule is the better one.

entries.label: an object a fold produced, used as a value object
entries.origin: the fold answering a value rather than a syntax node
entries.note: A fold whose result is a plain object used to answer nothing at all, so an expression that computed a nested value object deopted even though the engine had produced it correctly. Both rows reach the same declarations a written-out value object reaches, which is the claim: a folded object is as usable as one somebody typed, conditions and nesting included.

entries.label: an array a fold produced, as a fallback list and as a join receiver
entries.origin: the two array dispatch arms collapsing into one
entries.note: `s1` is the shape two dispatch arms disagreed about: one accepted `join` for a list the evaluation produced and the other refused it for the array literal a fold produced, so a mapped list could not be joined once the separator was a binding and the outer call fell to the older path. The fold answers the evaluator's own list now, so there is one arm. `s0` is the same value in the position that shows it whole -- a folded array expands into one declaration per entry, exactly as a written one does.

entries.label: a locale-sensitive method, refused here and folded upstream
entries.origin: issue 06, the exclusion the engine has no locale data for
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and the category the effort's spec sanctioned. Four measured reasons, each on its own sufficient. First, the engine's internationalisation feature reintroduces the exact dependency conflict that forced the engine to be vendored: the vendored tree relaxes two version bounds, and the feature pins roughly eleven more against the line the rest of the workspace is on. Second, that feature carries no compiled locale data and the provider crate is not vendored either, so building a locale context would fail at runtime unless this project shipped a data blob of its own. Third, it would not fix the number-formatting method regardless -- the engine ignores `toLocaleString`'s arguments unconditionally, with no feature gate at all. Fourth, with no locale argument the reference compiler takes the host's default, so its own answer is machine-dependent, and folding it would pin one build machine's value into every stylesheet the project ships. What the refusal costs is visible in the subject: upstream folds all four locale-sensitive methods against the host's full locale data, and the engine here answers `'i'.toLocaleUpperCase('tr')` as `I` where the language says `İ` -- so folding would emit a wrong declaration rather than no declaration. A refusal costs a build that would have compiled; a wrong fold costs a stylesheet nobody can find the fault in. `modules-06-locale-string-on-an-object` is the other row here. It is not the only such category on this branch, which is the spec sentence rather than this row: `modules-09-number-of-a-function` refuses a value with no compile-time form, `modules-09-string-of-the-environment-object` reads a missing option rather than a conversion, and `modules-12-amplification-across-a-chain` refuses a length it cannot read, each deliberately and each with its reason on the row. Which of the two counts stands is left to the decision record.

entries.label: a method call on a number written into the source
entries.origin: issue 06, the one receiver kind upstream cannot call a method on
entries.note: Both reject, in different words, which is what the parent spec's non-goal already asserts about this input -- so what is pinned here is that neither compiler compiles it, not either compiler's sentence. That is the half worth a regression test: without the guard this compiler would newly *fold* a method call on a written number and emit a declaration where the reference implementation fails the build, and no test outside the corpus would notice. A number a fold produced is a different shape and folds in both; see the chained-calls entry.

entries.label: a fold whose result is half a surrogate pair
entries.origin: issue 06, the UTF-16 divergence pinned rather than carried quietly
entries.note: Divergent in the class name only, and pinned rather than fixed. Slicing an astral pair leaves a lone low surrogate: well-formed UTF-16, and not a string any Rust `String` holds. The declaration text agrees, because upstream's own becomes a replacement character the moment the stylesheet is written to disk; the hash of the pre-encoding text does not. Refusing instead would fail a build upstream completes, and carrying the surrogate faithfully means a value type that holds WTF-8 through the whole pipeline — which is the same rewrite an indexed string read is waiting on.

entries.label: a length no declaration could use
entries.origin: issue 06, the allocation the engine does not bound itself; re-measured for issue 12
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and now configurably so. Upstream folds this at 200 MB of string. The engine bounds loop iterations, recursion and stack but not allocation, because growth inside a native builtin is not a counted loop, and building a string costs about 19 bytes of peak resident memory per code unit here -- so 200 million of them is gigabytes. A refusal turns a typo into a diagnostic instead of into the machine, and names both numbers so an author can tell a typo from a project that has outgrown the ceiling. The ceiling is `maxFoldedCharacters`, default 1000000: raise it past the count and the same source folds to the value upstream reaches.

entries.label: nesting past the configured evaluation depth
entries.origin: issue 06, the refusal that replaces a stack overflow
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, and configurably so. A hundred levels is past the shipped `maxEvaluationDepth` of 32, so this compiler refuses it with a message naming that number where upstream folds it to `.x16319ns`. The fold runs on a stack it claims for the configured depth, so the refusal is the setting rather than a bound of the fold's own: raise `maxEvaluationDepth` past the nesting and the same source folds to the same value upstream reaches. Re-measured against `@stylexjs/babel-plugin` 0.19.0 when the fold stopped carrying a ceiling of its own.

entries.label: a normalization the engine's Unicode tables do answer
entries.origin: issue 06, the exclusion that moved back into scope

entries.label: an amplifying call whose receiver is itself a call
entries.origin: issue 12, the rule that keeps per-link bounds from multiplying
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and the one length a readable count is still not enough to bound. The ceiling is compared against the length the call would build, which for `repeat` is the count times the receiver's own length -- and a receiver that is itself a call has no length the guard can read without evaluating it, which is exactly what bounding each link separately fails to prevent. Two counts of a thousand are each far inside the ceiling and their product is a million. Upstream folds this. A named receiver is not this case: a name holding a string has a length that can be read, and `base.repeat(3)` folds.

entries.label: an array length declared by an argument
entries.origin: issue 18, the allocation the ceilings reached too late
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and configurably so. `Array(n)` declares how long its array will be and allocates nothing for it -- the array is sparse -- so the cost lands on whichever call in the chain first touches it, and the entry ceiling used to read the length only where the array crossed back. `Array(100000000).fill(0)` therefore spent thirty-four seconds and four hundred megabytes of resident memory before refusing, and `Array(100000000).includes(1)` folded in thirteen seconds with no ceiling having measured anything at all. The bound is now read where the length is declared, so the same refusal costs milliseconds. The ceiling is `maxFoldedEntries`, default 10000: raise it past the declared length and the same source folds to the value upstream reaches. `Array.from({length: n})` is the same declaration one property along and is bounded with it.

entries.label: an array length only a string comes back from
entries.origin: issue 18, the capability reading a length at its declaration trades away
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and the price of the row above. The entry ceiling used to bound entries that *crossed back*, so an array built and joined inside the engine was bounded only by the string it came to -- which is how `Array(100000000).join(',')` came to spend twenty seconds building an array nothing had measured before a string ceiling caught the text. Reading the length where it is declared closes that, and costs this shape: ten thousand and one commas is a string well inside `maxFoldedCharacters`, and upstream folds it. The ceiling is `maxFoldedEntries`, and raising it past the declared length folds the same source to upstream's value.

entries.label: an array length declared inside a callback
entries.origin: issue 18, the length no ceiling could bound; re-measured for issue 21
entries.note: Both fold, and to the same value -- the row is kept as the subject rather than as a divergence. It was recorded as one because a callback body is evaluated once per element of a receiver nothing in front of the engine had measured, so a length written into the source bounded one evaluation rather than the call. The receiver's element count is now read where it can be, and both rules compare the product: two elements times a declared length of two is four, which is four orders of magnitude inside `maxFoldedEntries`. What still refuses is the remainder the blanket rule stood in for -- a receiver whose element count cannot be read, which the row below pins, and a declared length the guard cannot read at all, where the unreadable half is the length rather than the repeats.

entries.label: an amplifying call inside a callback over a receiver nothing counted
entries.origin: issue 21, the remainder the blanket refusal stood in for
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and not a configured ceiling: no value of either allocation option folds these. Both rules now bound a length written inside a callback by the receiver's element count times the length, so what is left is the pair of readings that count comes from. `s0` is a declared length the guard cannot read -- it arrives through a parameter -- and refusing it is what keeps `[{length: 100000000}].map(x => Array.from(x).length)` from spending sixty-eight seconds before a ceiling notices. `s1` is an element count the guard will not read: the receiver is itself a call, whose answer is bounded per link, and reading it is what would let two allowed counts multiply into one that is neither -- the same rule `modules-12` applies to a chained receiver's own length. Upstream folds both. Written on an array whose elements are in the source, each folds here too, which the row above pins.

entries.label: a string grown past the ceiling by `+`
entries.origin: issue 20, the character ceiling reaching a string the evaluator grows
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and configurably so. `maxFoldedCharacters` bounds what a fold builds and what it carries, and both readings sit where a value crosses the engine -- so nothing looked at `a + a`, which the evaluator answers itself. A chain of ten such lines from this base folded to 102,400,000 characters in three seconds, past a ceiling a hundred times smaller, bounded only by the *depth* budget, which limits how far a walk descends rather than how large a value gets. The bound now sits on the growth: each `+` is measured against the same ceiling before the copy that joins its operands, so the refusal arrives before the next doubling allocates rather than after. The chain here is the reported one, at a base chosen so that upstream's answer -- `1000448px` -- is only just past the default ceiling: the shape is what the row is for, and a base that made upstream build a hundred megabytes would buy nothing. Upstream bounds none of this and folds it. Raise `maxFoldedCharacters` past the length and the same source folds to upstream's value.

entries.label: a string grown past the ceiling by an interpolation
entries.origin: issue 20, the second expression the evaluator grows a string with
entries.note: Acceptance divergent for the reason the row above is, on the other of the two expressions the evaluator grows a string with itself. A template is bounded by the same number and measured the same way -- each quasi and each interpolation against the running total -- so a template that passes the ceiling refuses at the piece that passes it. `concat` and `repeat` needed nothing: both are calls, and the fold already bounds a call on the way in and on the way back, which is why the bound went on the growth rather than on what a binding may hold. Upstream folds this too, and raising `maxFoldedCharacters` past the length folds it here.

entries.label: an array joined past the ceiling by an interpolation
entries.origin: issue 23, the character ceiling reaching the join an array's `ToString` performs
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and configurably so. Two hundred elements of nine hundred thousand characters join to 180,000,199 -- a hundred and eighty times the default ceiling -- and upstream folds them to `180000199px` in well under a second, because the join it builds is never materialised. This compiler refuses, and the number is `maxFoldedCharacters`: raise it past the length and the same source folds to upstream's value. What changed with issue 23 is not the verdict but when it arrives. The refusal already named the right ceiling, and it named it after rendering every element and joining them -- 3.9 seconds on this spelling and 7.5 on the `+` one, since each element's `ToString` copies a string the value already holds and the join copies them all again. The join is now written into the measured buffer element by element, so the refusal costs the element that passed the ceiling and nothing after it: 65 milliseconds here and 92 on the row below. The separator counts as part of what is built, so two four-character elements are nine characters.

entries.label: an array joined past the ceiling by `+`
entries.origin: issue 23, the second expression an array's join reaches the ceiling through
entries.note: Acceptance divergent for the reason the row above is, on the other of the two expressions the evaluator grows a string with itself. Two hundred elements of nine hundred thousand characters join to 180,000,199 -- a hundred and eighty times the default ceiling -- and upstream folds them to `180000199px` in well under a second, because the join it builds is never materialised. Both operands of a `+` now grow one buffer, so an array on either side is measured as it joins rather than after -- and the sentence names the concatenation, because an author looking for what grew the string has the expression they wrote rather than the join inside it. Raising `maxFoldedCharacters` past the length folds this too.

entries.label: a call through a name whose argument is another one
entries.origin: issue 24, an argument that is itself a call through a name
entries.note: Identical, and the divergence this row was written for is closed. The dispatch answered a call through a name by handing back the arrow the name holds, and the style-value position applied it -- so the answer depended on who asked. The same call one argument deeper arrived at the arrow as a function no parameter could bind, which left the body unevaluated and reported an internal expectation about a binary operand. The call is now applied where it is written, and an array argument binds as the array it is rather than as nothing.

entries.label: a number reached through an array's join
entries.origin: issue 25, the join `ToNumber` reaches its number through
entries.note: Identical, and the cost this row was written for is gone. `ToNumber` of an array is `ToNumber` of its join, and the number bridge collected it: the two hundred elements above spent 10.2 seconds and 180 MB reaching upstream's own `NaN`. A bound alone would have made that a refusal where upstream folds, so the bridge reads what the ceiling bounds instead -- `ToNumber` keeps no string, and its only question is whether the text spells a numeric literal, so the text is dropped at the first character no numeric literal holds. A comma is such a character, which settles an array of two or more elements at its first separator. What the ceiling is left bounding is a text still numeric at a million characters, and no expression can build one: every way of growing a string is bounded by the same number, so the only route to it is a literal of a million digits written out. That half is pinned as a test rather than as a row here, since the source would be the megabyte it measures.

entries.label: an array result longer than a declaration could use
entries.origin: issue 06, the second half of the allocation bound; re-measured for issue 12
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately, and configurably so. A string short enough to build becomes one array element per code unit, and an element costs about 190 bytes of peak resident memory against a code unit's one or two, so the count that reaches a literal is bounded by a ceiling of its own. Upstream folds this. The ceiling is `maxFoldedEntries`, default 10000: raise it past the count and the same source folds.

entries.label: a length written as an expression rather than a number
entries.origin: issue 06, the cost of bounding a count by reading it; re-measured for issue 12
entries.note: Identical, and the divergence this row was written for is closed. The count used to have to be written into the source as a number, so a count computed from an expression refused even when it was small. It is now bounded by being read -- through the evaluator and then the language's own ToNumber -- so an expression, a name and a literal all reach the same arithmetic. The bound itself did not move: the ceiling is compared against the length the call would build, which for `repeat` is the count times the receiver's own length.

entries.label: toLocaleString on a receiver that carries no locale
entries.origin: issue 06, the agreed object method the locale exclusion costs
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, and the one method on the ticket's agreed object list that does not fold. `toLocaleString` carries no locale on an object -- it delegates to `toString` -- but it formats on a number, and which of the two a receiver will produce is not knowable before evaluating it. One name cannot be both admitted and refused, so it is refused and this is the cost.

entries.label: `String()` of the environment object
entries.origin: ticket 09, the globals that fold by being called
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, and no longer about the conversion. The environment object is this compiler's own value, so the engine never sees it and the conversion behind the fold answers for it — with `[object Object]`, as upstream does. What this row still reads is the subject compiling with no `env` option set, where there is no environment object to convert at all and the refusal names the missing configuration. Configured, the two agree, which `string_of_the_environment_object` pins.

entries.label: `String()` of a token group and of a token reference
entries.origin: ticket 09, the globals that fold by being called
entries.note: Identical. A value the bridge cannot carry no longer refuses the call: the engine is handed JavaScript values, this compiler has values of its own, and the conversion behind the fold answers for those through the same coercion `+` and an interpolation use. So the two conversion implementations no longer serve disjoint positions, and a value cannot read one way in a call and another in a template. Upstream folds the group to its variable-group hash and a member of it to the `var(...)` the token names, and both now fold to the same class names and rule text here — measured against `@stylexjs/babel-plugin`. entries.label: a property read that leads onto the language's function graph
entries.origin: issue 15, found by the generated sweep
entries.note: Acceptance divergent, deliberately. `constructor` is an own property of every prototype the sweep crosses, and no curated row had named it -- upstream folds both of these, since a string's `constructor` is `String` and an array's is `Array`. What the refusal holds back is the step after: `String`'s own `constructor` is `Function`, which compiles a string into a function, so `"".constructor.constructor("return Date.now()").call()` is a chain of two property reads and a call -- shapes every other rule here admits -- whose answer is a different number on every build and whose body can assign to `String.prototype` in an engine every later fold shares. `call`, `apply` and `bind` are refused with it because they turn an unapplied function back into a call. Folding the harmless half means admitting the read that reaches the harmful one, since the guard cannot know which `constructor` a chain will land on before evaluating it.

entries.label: an array method whose callback is reached through a name
entries.origin: issue 15, found by the generated sweep; closed by issue 19
entries.note: Agreement, and it was acceptance divergent until issue 19. A callback written out in place folded -- issue 10 prints it and the engine runs it -- while the same arrow reached through a name refused, because what crosses the bridge inward is a value and a function has no value form to carry. What crosses for a function instead is the declaration it came from, printed back as the default of the parameter the name became: the engine binds the name where the module bound it, so a callback parameter of the same spelling shadows it exactly as it did in the source. Which declarations qualify is decided by what the name resolves to, and the set is upstream's own -- an arrow with plain parameters and a single expression body, never written to after it was declared -- so a block body, a destructured or defaulted parameter, a `function` of either spelling and a reassigned binding are refused on both sides. Those refusals now name the binding rather than the call, since the method is not what an author has to change.

entries.label: a call whose callee is a name rather than a member

entries.note: Agreement, and it was acceptance divergent until issue 22. Distinct from the shape issue 19 closed, which is a callback *passed* by name: these two call a function through a name, and nothing about the function was ever unreachable -- `inner` resolved and crossed exactly as issue 19 made it. What was missing was the admission of the callee, and what decides it is where the call sits. The outermost call stays the dispatch below the fold, which resolves a name this compiler's own way -- a dynamic style's own parameters and the injected function map are answered there, and measured, that path already folds `inner('a')` to this rule. A call *inside* an expression the fold claimed has no second answer, since handing one back hands back the whole expression around it and the method that would have re-run a callback body moved into the engine. The declaration set is unchanged, because the carriage is: a block body, a `function` of either spelling and a reassigned binding still refuse on both sides, naming the binding.

entries.label: an array method whose callback names a StyleX function
entries.origin: issue 17, reported while building issue 10
entries.note: Agreement, and it was acceptance divergent until issue 17. The injected function map is not JavaScript, so it cannot be carried into the engine -- but `firstThatWorks` answers from its arguments and touches nothing else, so it crosses as a function the engine may call, built over the same ordering core the evaluator's own path uses. That is what makes the callback the engine's job again: the array methods that would have run it moved into the engine in issue 06 and the function had not, so the whole declaration refused. `s2` is the same call outside any callback, whose answer is a fold's receiver, and it refused for the same reason. A StyleX function that writes into the build -- `keyframes` hashes a rule and injects it -- is still refused inside a callback, and so is one read as a value rather than called: both remain acceptance divergent and are pinned in `transform_stylex_create_test/stylex_functions_in_a_fold.rs`.
